newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS-Hungary high leads E.Europe bourses in week.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hungary high leads E.Europe bourses in week.

text.p: An optimistic earnings outlook for Hungarian firms helped the Budapest bourse post an all-time high this week, while Czech stocks edged up but Warsaw fell due to a heavy flow of primary market issues.
Elsewhere, Croatian shares rose and the Romanian indices hit year highs but other regional bourses saw losses.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian shares, rose 0.5 percent.
BUDAPEST

Hungarian shares hit an all-time high on Wednesday. Although profit-taking later trimmed some of the gains and further corrections were likely, traders said the long-term outlook remained positive, thanks to strong earnings.
"It (the market) remains fairly well supported," said Roger Monson, chief equity strategist at Daiwa Europe Ltd.
"I wouldn't expect a large correction even if you have some sort of weakness in nearby markets in Prague or Warsaw."
Despite profit-taking on Friday on a number of shares, the market edged up, bolstered by large-cap oil and gas firm MOL.
PRAGUE
Czech shares edged slightly higher in the week but volume was thin.
The highlight of the week was the return of SPT Telecom, the most heavily weighted Czech share, accounting for 19.7 percent of the offical PX50 index's capitalisation.
SPT had been suspended ahead of its annual general meeting and its return heralded a pickup in activity as well as solid gains.
"Recently, I've read a series of surveys from recognised brokerage firms...and everyone says that people should be overweight on Telecom," said Radek Vavra of Citicorp Securities.
On Friday, SPT announced a 10-for-one stock split which dealers said could further boost the issue's prospects.
WARSAW
Polish shares fell 2.6 percent this week to 16,048.1 points after last week's gain and analysts said the market was locked in its three-month horizontal trend amid conflicting signals.

Analysts said May earnings data released this week were mediocre but that optimism over Wednesday's news that the privatisation offer of large Bank Handlowy was heavily oversubscribed cheered the market.

Analysts said much of the money mobilised in the Handlowy oversubscription could go to the public offering of copper giant KGHM Polska Miedz SA starting in late June, though enough should go to stocks to prevent steep falls by the main index.
ZAGREB

Croatian stocks closed mixed on Friday after firming earlier in the week, seemingly buoyed by Franjo Tudjman's victory in presidential polls, and analysts predicted more mild growth for the days ahead.

Leading issues fared poorly on Friday. Drugs firm Pliva, pending the publication of its annual results, did not trade, while Zagrebacka Banka's ordinaries lost 35 kuna to 2,000, with only 100 shares sold.
BUCHAREST
Most Bucharest stocks rose this week and traders expected a rally early next week which could be followed by corrections thereafter.
Three independent market indices climbed to new year highs. The CAS-SE index, launched by Romania-based Creditanstalt Securities, closed up 9.79 percent.
BRATISLAVA
The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) continued in listless trading activity this week and brokers expected no significant turn for the better in the short and medium terms.
The 16-share SAX index fell 6.24 points, or 3.53 percent, to close at new year-low of 170.70 points on Friday.
"There are no domestic players on the market at the moment and the foreign investors are cautious over the possibility of devaluation of the crown," Libor Briska of Creditanstalt said.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares slipped 1.21 percent this week as the blue-chip SBI index fell 14.93 points to 1,200.8. Turnover rose to 266.7 million tolars ($1.7 million) from 235.7 million.

"I expect shares to fall gradually on poor volumes over the summer -- activity would be boosted by any news about EU treaty ratification. In a matter of a few days after the news the index could move up or down by 10 percent," said Goran Brankovic, a trader of Nova Ljubljanska Banka.

Two weeks ago the constitutional court delayed the ratification of the treaty, which was signed in June last year, and ordered parliament to change the country's constitution in order to allow foreigners to own real-estate.
